beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The Illness Machine examines why care can help while harmful conditions remain unchanged.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: It follows how money, childhood, workplaces, and institutions enter the causes of distress.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The book’s distinctive question is which conditions cause illness, trigger it, or prolong it.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Readers gain a way to examine social causes alongside biological vulnerability and clinical care.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The opening follows a study of children in western North Carolina.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Casino profits funded annual payments to members of the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Some previously poor families crossed the poverty line after those payments began.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Children in those families showed fewer conduct and oppositional defiant symptoms.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Anxiety and depression did not show the same improvement in that study.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Earlier assessments let researchers compare each group before and after the income change.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The book uses that selective result to ask which pathways money actually changes.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: In another example, panic begins after a supervisor makes shifts unpredictable and humiliates workers.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The clinic can offer care, while the same workplace keeps recreating exposure.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The book asks what the employer controls: schedules, workload, voice, and safe reporting.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: It proposes immediate clinical help alongside changes to conditions that sustain harmful exposure.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The task is to reduce harmful exposure while helping the person now.
